Andrew Skurka on Pro Tips for Older Hikers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In my 20s, I was a dirtbag thru-hiker.
  • According to recent reports, for the last 17 years of my life, I’ve been running a guided backpacking service.
  • If you’re watching this video before Saturday, December 5th, 2026, and if you live in the Denver metro area, I invite you to join us for a live Backpacker Radio episode at the Skylark Lounge in Denver.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hi, I’m Andrew Skurka. In my 20s, I was a dirtbag thru-hiker. I was the first person to do the C2C Route, the Great Western Loop, and the Alaska-Yukon Expedition.

According to recent reports, for the last 17 years of my life, I’ve been running a guided backpacking service. Every year, I get to go to places like southern Utah, Alaska, Yellowstone, and the High Sierra to teach other people backpacking skills.

If you’re watching this video before Saturday, December 5th, 2026, and if you live in the Denver metro area, I invite you to join us for a live Backpacker Radio episode at the Skylark Lounge in Denver.

It has been revealed that and if you’re looking to have an exceptional backpacking experience in 2027, please consider joining me on one of my guided backpacking trips. We are accepting applications starting Monday, December 7th, 2026. For more information, you can learn more here.

According to recent reports, today’s video is geared toward backpackers who are getting up there in age. I’m going to help set your expectations about what’s to come and also give you ideas about how to keep backpacking fun late into life.

Recent findings suggest that now, importantly, I should mention I’m not old at 45, but I do work with a lot of older backpackers. And I think what’s fair to say, too, is that at 45, I’ve been backpacking for over half my life, since 21.

And backpacking for me has changed as I’ve gotten older, and I expect that it will continue to change as I get into my 50s and 60s and 70s.

It has been revealed that in some respects, backpacking gets easier as you get older. So specifically, you tend to have more money, you have more time, and you’re probably more motivated because you know that the window of opportunity is closing.

But mostly, for backpackers who are getting older, the key takeaway should be that backpacking is going to get harder physically.

In a recent development, putting in those miles, hiking all that vertical, trying to recover overnight, sleeping on the ground—none of that gets easier as you get into your 50s, 60s, and 70s. It was much easier when you were in your sprightly 20s and 30s.

Recent findings suggest that so the key thing that I would say to an older backpacker is, what are you going to do? Are you going to stop backpacking? Or are you going to make some adaptations and some tweaks to your approach to make sure that you can keep backpacking late into life?

Photo courtesy of Andrew Skurka.

Let me put this conversation into context by giving you some statistics from our guided trip program.

According to recent reports, so every year, we have about 400 to 500 clients on our trips. And I’ll give you some specific data from 2026, although these patterns haven’t changed a lot in many years.

In 2026, 24% of our clients were in their 50s, 23% of our clients were in their 60s, and only 4% of our clients were in their 70s.

Sources indicate that I’m not in my 70s, but I do have 70-year-old parents and 70-year-old in-laws. I don’t want to speculate about what might be happening in the 70s that’s responsible for that massive drop-off.

But to anyone who’s approaching this phase of life, this empty-nester, retiree stage of life, just realize that the window will close.

So if you have goals, if you have backpacking goals, just make sure not to wait too long on them because as you get older and older, backpacking definitely seems to get more difficult and participation rates go down.

There are certainly exceptions to these demographic trends that I just gave you.

I would call out, for example, Greybeard, who at 91 just became the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail. But he’s a freak. He’s a total freak. He’s such an outlier.

For the average backpacker, for the average person, I would expect that your backpacking interests will fade during your 60s or into your early 70s.

Let’s talk about the physical challenges of backpacking and how you can mitigate or adapt to them.

As we get older, the first reckoning is that putting in the same amount of miles and the same amount of vertical that we did when we were younger just gets harder.

You can push into it, but you’re not going to recover as promptly, and the time it takes you to do those miles and that vertical is going to be longer, which cuts into camp time.

So you might not like the solution, but I just think it’s realistic: You need to start planning less ambitious itineraries.

Relatedly, but it’s a little bit more specific, one thing that we really observe with our older clients is a loss of power and strength.

Recent findings suggest that we see this mostly when climbing up hills. An older client who keeps up with the group no problem on flat terrain or downhill will just move toward the back of the pack on those long, extended climbs.

They just no longer have that power and that strength, that horsepower to push uphill and carry their bodies and their packs against gravity.

Industry observers note that so the solution here, part of it, again, is similar to the first solution. Maybe just be a little less ambitious in your planning.

Recent findings suggest that but you also can mitigate that by doing more uphill-specific training. You can also add weight training into your mix of exercises.

And then one little technique change is that instead of taking those big, long, powerful strides that you may have taken in your youth, shorten your stride and increase your cadence.

According to recent reports, I started doing this years ago, even, and I just found that it put a lot less pressure on my joints and on my muscles. I didn’t feel nearly as worked at the end of the day by those big, long extensions that require a lot of power and strength in my muscles.

It has been revealed that among our older clients, we also see a loss of agility and finesse. And this becomes apparent on any kind of uneven walking surface: talus, scree, scrambles, slickrock.

There are some solutions to this.

One is just to take those sections a little bit more slowly and with more caution.

Another way to manage it, if you’re not already, is that you should definitely be adding trekking poles to your kit. These will give you just a little bit of extra stability. It’s like now you have four legs instead of just two. So some extra stability.

And then one last thing you can do, and you can integrate this into your training, is to emphasize balance.

According to recent reports, so do exercises that require balance, for example, one-legged squats or exercises on a BOSU ball. Anything to kind of increase that sensitivity about your position in the air and things that strengthen all those connective ligaments and muscles.

A fourth observation of our older clients, and when we’re talking about old, most people are thinking 50s, 60s, but I will say just as a 45-year-old who has been running since high school, one of the massive differences that I see as I get on in age is just the lack of recovery.

In my 20s, I’ll just, here’s a remarkable number, even today.

Sources indicate that so when I did the Great Western Loop, it was 208 days, and I averaged 33 miles a day. I was 27 years old.

According to recent reports, I cannot at this age fathom hiking that many miles per day, day after day after day. I definitely feel like that sustained effort, that wear and tear, would break me at this point.

So longer recovery, or less efficient recovery, should just be the expectation among older backpackers.

Here are a couple of things that you can do.

First is that you can build recovery days into your itinerary.

Sources indicate that so maybe days one, two, three are normal. Maybe day four is a little bit easier. And that way you can be strong again on days five and six.

Or maybe you’re just a little bit more patient with your trips.

Industry observers note that so if you’re going on, say, a seven-day trip, days one, two, three, you finish the day still feeling like there’s plenty more left in the tank. And that way you can be strong on days four, five, and six.

Sources indicate that in comparison, a younger person would charge out of the gate and would be able to recover well enough to remain strong throughout the trip. That just doesn’t happen as you age.

So building in some recovery would be one option.

The second thing you can do is create itineraries that have some flexibility in them.

Industry observers note that so this is a little bit more difficult to do with point-to-point itineraries. For example, if you’re going to do a section of, say, the Colorado Trail, it’s easier to do if you initiative a loop.

And if you proposal that loop, just identify some places where you can go where you can add some distance and some vertical, but also places where you can shorten your route, too.

And that way, if you’re not recovering, if you feel like you need an easy day but you need to stay on an itinerary, you have that kind of built in.

The third thing you can do to help with recovery is that you should be carrying plenty of ibuprofen.

Use this with some care. It can create some kidney issues, so just be aware of the limits on how much ibuprofen you can take in. But ibuprofen is an anti-inflammatory. It will help with some recovery.

And then one more thing you can do to help your recovery is just emphasize self-care when you’re out on the trail.

I’m not necessarily, like, I have seen clients carry foam rollers to give themselves a little bit of a massage at night.

You could also be taking ice baths if you can find cold water. You might do some light stretching in the morning before you get going.

But just anything to kind of take it easier on your body and let your body endure that stress and strain better than if you just kind of raw-dogged it.

Everyone’s gonna love that I just said raw dog.

The fifth experience you might have as an older backpacker is that you’re getting less restful sleep.

And I’ll say this as someone whose wife woke them up multiple times last night because I was apparently snoring so loud.

So here are a couple of solutions for you.

First, if you are not already using a plush, thick, warm sleeping pad, with the Therm-a-Rest NeoAir XLite being, I would say, like a minimum, you should go ahead and do that.

So upgrade from your Therm-a-Rest RidgeRest or your Therm-a-Rest Z Lite. That’s for some other generation now. Get something comfortable to sleep on.

The second thing you can do is bring a pee bottle with you, for the folks who can’t hold it as well as they used to.

It has been revealed that have a dedicated pee bottle. You can bring this into your shelter at night, and that way you don’t have to go outside in the middle of the night when you have to go pee.

You can just pee in your bottle, put it off to the side, and go back to bed.

In addition to the sleeping pad, you also want to make sure that you’ve got a nice pillow.

In my 20s, on all my big, long thru-hikes, I slept on lots of things that no normal person would ever want to sleep on.

I would use my nasty shoes. I would sleep on bags of trash, like wrapper trash from candy bars and energy bar wrappers. I would sleep on my water bottles. Anything to give my head a little bit of a lift.

And nowadays, I can’t do that, though.

So I have a real air pillow. It’s about that wide, that tall, it’s like two and a half, three inches thick.

Better than not having one, for sure.

And then the last thing, if you have sleep apnea, there are lightweight CPAP machines out there.

So you can do some research, and if that makes the difference, I mean, they still weigh a couple of pounds, but if that makes the difference between you sleeping well at night and being able to backpack for an extended period of time, or you trying to go backpacking and you never get a good night’s rest and the maximum trip duration is like three days before you’re just utterly exhausted and have a bad attitude because you’re not sleeping well, then carry the four-pound machine and move on with your life.

Just accept that as part of being older.

You should also be thinking about what you can do to make your camping experience more comfortable.

So one easy solution would be to at least bring a sit pad.

Even better, maybe investing one pound-ish in a nice camp chair that allows you to sit 12 inches or 15 inches off the ground as opposed to having to sit on the ground.

Good little trick if you haven’t already, though: If you’re carrying a bear canister, which would be required equipment in places like the High Sierra or Rocky Mountain, you can also use your bear canister as a camp chair.

Also think about the type of shelter that you’re using.

As an older person, you don’t really want to be, or like to be, crawling on the ground, and you don’t have as much flexibility.

So shelters that have a side entry are way better than shelters that have an entry at the head.

And also, give yourself a shelter with a little bit of additional interior room.

Instead of maybe doing the Hyperlite Mountain Gear Mid 1, which is a wonderful shelter, I use it most of the summer, maybe instead get a Zpacks Duplex, which is for two people.

It’ll give you a little bit of extra room to move around, and you’ll feel a little bit less cramped.

So that way you can sit in your shelter and spend time in your shelter more comfortably.

The last thing that I hear from our older clients is that their feet start to change shape.

So specifically, they get a little bit wider, which might have something to do with the fact that their arches start collapsing and their feet start to get flatter.

And the last thing that happens is that the fat pads on the underside of their feet become thinner.

So a lot of our older clients tend to gravitate toward a more cushioned shoe like this one.

If you notice with this shoe, just look at this substantial, fat foam midsole that wraps all the way around the shoe.

This ends up being a more cushioned, comfortable thing to wear. Maybe the analogy, it’s a little bit like driving a Cadillac.

There’s a lot more that goes into selecting a shoe than just the midsole cushioning, but all things being equal, if you have two shoes that fit well and that are well-suited for your application, but one has a thicker midsole than the other, maybe gravitate toward this one.

As we age, we tend to lose our strength or power, and we also tend to lose our balance.

So as an older backpacker, one really easy way to mitigate that is you could just lean hard into the ultralight gear thing.

Twenty-three years ago, I actually was an intern for GoLite in the summer of 2002, and I remember at that time GoLite wasn’t getting a lot of traction in the backpacking community, except for among older hikers.

Because for them, they saw that GoLite was creating gear, and it was an approach that allowed them to backpack later into their life.

Because at the time, think about backpacking, everyone backpacked like NOLS or Outward Bound, with these huge packs that weighed 50, 60 pounds.

That was just totally ordinary.

So GoLite was sort of pitching this alternative, and a lot of the older backpackers saw the possibilities.

I have older backpackers, older clients, who have gone like crazy with the lightweight gear.

They’re the ones who usually show up with the lightest packs because they usually have the most discretionary income.

I have a couple of clients who, it’s like, it’s DCF shelters, it’s DCF stuff sacks, it’s DCF bear hangs.

I think that if they could find it, they probably would buy DCF underwear.

I mean, they have just gone full in on ultralight gear.

Sources indicate that that’s not to say that you need or can buy a bunch of DCF gear. If your financial means are a little bit more limited, there are actually a lot of free ways to lighten up your pack.

Here are a couple of things I would suggest.

One is that before you buy anything, you do a lot of homework.

You really understand the likely conditions that you will encounter, and you really have a heart-to-heart with yourself about what your backpacking style is going to be.

See another video that we’ve done about that.

And then you just buy the right stuff the first time instead of having to cycle through gear that isn’t quite what you thought it was going to be.

So that’d be number one: Just buy right the first time.

You can also just not buy a lot of gear.

Part of lightening up is just taking only things that you need, and that results in you not having to spend money on things that are extraneous and discretionary and that actually don’t help your backpacking experience at all.

And my last tip for saving money on gear would be to buy equipment that is versatile.

So buy equipment that will be appropriate for a wide range of conditions and locations, and that way you can just have one kit that’s kind of a jack of all trades, that tends to work pretty well in all of the locations where you might want to backpack.

I’ve talked about the physical challenges that older backpackers face and how to mitigate or address some of them.

I’ve also talked about the importance of lightweight equipment.

The last thing that I’d like to talk about to close is the importance of shifting your mindset toward backpacking as you age.

Let me just tell you, from a personal perspective.

In my 20s and 30s, I was a hard-charging backpacker.

It was dawn to dusk every day, as many miles as I could do, as much vertical as I could do.

I just leaned into that, the physical challenge of backpacking.

I wanted to see as much as I possibly could with a limited amount of time, and I wore it like a badge of honor if I could hike 35 or 40 miles a day.

As I’ve gotten older and my body is less cooperative with that approach to backpacking, I have just accepted that backpacking can look different.

I have leaned into other aspects of the backpacking experience.

I have become a much more capable companion while backpacking instead of just being sort of a thorny soloist.

I have leaned into all the interpretive opportunities of backpacking.

Sources indicate that I’ve learned about birds. I’ve learned about geology. I’ve learned about history. I’ve learned about archaeology.

And then I also have just started to love even more the peace and quiet that backpacking gives me.

So my spring usually starts with a backpacking trip in southern Utah, and the thing that I always respond to when I go out there is just how quiet and peaceful it is out there.

And that’s just such a welcome break from my ordinary life.

And even though in the spring in Utah I’m no longer doing those 35- or 40-mile days, I love backpacking just as much.

I just am loving it in different ways.

Maybe in short, the thing to think about as an older backpacker is that just getting out is a win.

I was a little wary of doing this video just because, as a 45-year-old, I don’t want to give the appearance that I’m telling older backpackers what life is going to be like or what they should be doing.

But hopefully you have learned a thing or two.

I would love for the comment section in this video to get lit up with tips and tricks from older backpackers who can share their hard-earned wisdom with others.

Industry observers note that we’ll see you next week, Monday at noon. Thanks.

A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great major-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains.
  • Sources indicate that the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great major-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

Sources indicate that the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a upcoming route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

In a recent development, three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential upcoming line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Crossing a scree slope on Pik Breeze.

Beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

It has been revealed that canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

They climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

They called their new line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

Later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’.

According to recent reports, three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

Recent findings suggest that skalec and Vitez also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic and Sinisa Skalec about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats the Central Route on a peak called Small Russian Tower.

Sources indicate that was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

It has been revealed that eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

This significantly hindered our climbing, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

In a recent development, one thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

According to recent reports, can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

In a recent development, the two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

Recent findings suggest that another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

According to recent reports, here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

Recent findings suggest that presently, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

How many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

According to recent reports, during the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia….

Why did your group decide to go there?

We had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive substantial walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

Are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

Industry observers note that yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

In a recent development, some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

According to recent reports, patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

It has been revealed that climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least on the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

Industry observers note that the granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in the Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

You climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

There were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

Industry observers note that from there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

At the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

It has been revealed that all belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

As in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

How much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

The most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a latest route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

In a recent development, your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

Most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other significant-wall areas?

Sources indicate that we were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

Hiker Dies Trying To Help Son Amid Icy Conditions on Mt. Baden-Powell

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A hiker died Sunday morning on Southern California’s Mt.
  • A GoFundMe arranged by the victim’s niece identifies the deceased as ultrarunner Guillermo Alejandro Batres and says he had been attempting to help his son, who had slipped and fallen, when he himself lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.
  • According to recent reports, authorities have not confirmed the victim’s identity or cause of death and have not released additional details about the incident.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A hiker died Sunday morning on Southern California’s Mt. Baden-Powell after slipping on ice and falling roughly 500 feet, according to AV Scanner News, a local Southern California emergency news-monitoring page.

A GoFundMe arranged by the victim’s niece identifies the deceased as ultrarunner Guillermo Alejandro Batres and says he had been attempting to help his son, who had slipped and fallen, when he himself lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

According to recent reports, authorities have not confirmed the victim’s identity or cause of death and have not released additional details about the incident. According to AV Scanner News, the fatal accident occurred roughly 3 miles up the trail from Vincent Gap and “family members of the hiker were also reported to be at the scene.”.

Los Angeles County Fire Department and Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department Palmdale Station responded to the incident and an air unit was used to recover Batres’s remains.

Mt. Baden-Powell is a 9,407-foot summit in the Angeles National Forest. The summit lies 0.1 miles off the Pacific Crest Trail at northbound mile 377.9 and is a popular destination for PCT hikers and Los Angeles residents alike. Snow and ice can make the route treacherous during the winter months.

Featured image: View of Mt. Baden Powell and Angeles Crest Highway. Photo: Diego Acuna.

#159508. Latest Update: Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (795 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • According to recent reports, with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Sources indicate that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

According to recent reports, with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Sources indicate that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

Last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

Sources indicate that the skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

In a recent development, the accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

Other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police said the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

Recent findings suggest that avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident shows that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

Recent findings suggest that the accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

According to recent reports, the avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

The second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

Fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the big powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

After a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them blueprint to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

Sources indicate that snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) shows low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

The avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps reveals remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.

Family Offers $75,000 Reward to Save Climber Missing on Mount Fuji

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (158 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police announced that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun.
  • In a recent development, his two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment.
  • His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police announced that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

In a recent development, his two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

Tech Report: Climbers Forge Newly introduced Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the new route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).
  • Industry observers note that expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited.
  • Siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the new route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).

Industry observers note that expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited. After returning home, however, Stefan Siegrist reported the details, and the team’s cameraman, Christoph Detschmann, posted a video summary of the expedition:.

Siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge. At the end of September, he, Sala, and Bosshard reached base camp in the Kishtwar massif.

It has been revealed that the three Swiss climbers were prepared to endure a long period of bad weather while acclimatizing. To their surprise, a good weather window opened right away. It was too good to let go, despite not being properly acclimatized and Sala and Bosshard’s lack of altitude experience. The window was expected to last just three days. After many “discussions and doubts,” they left base camp on October 3.

Recent findings suggest that sala had a headache during the first night, but the following morning, they were all totally focused on the climb, and the tension disappeared. “We assumed that we were unlikely to reach the summit on this attempt, and that we would therefore be wasting our only chance before a major storm [brought] the season to an end,” Siegrist explained. “So from then on, the idea was simply to climb higher and acclimatize, without any pressure.”.

A moment of the climb, filmed from a drone by Christoph Detschmann.

Along the way, they discovered they had left their stove at base camp. No problem in 2026: The expedition photographer used his drone to carry the stove up to them. The use of drones was a hot topic during the recent Piolets d’Or: To what extent are they compatible with alpine-style criteria? While most accepted that drones could scout routes or sections out of view of base camp, many considered using them to carry equipment up a face to be a red line.

On Shiva, Siegrist says the delivery of the missing stove “proved essential to the success of the climb.”.

Sources indicate that the climbers spent their second night at 5,250m at the base of the northwest ridge. On the following morning, they had to decide whether to continue or retreat. They all felt well, but starting the highly technical ridge was a point of no return. At the same time, Siegrist recalls, they realized they really had a chance to summit. And so on they went.

That night, they stopped at 5,700m in what Siegrist describes as a crucial moment. His partners had not been at that altitude before, and the latest forecast confirmed a storm the following day. They decided to wait and see what the morning looked like. No one slept at all that night.

Recent findings suggest that the last meters before the summit. Drone image by Christoph Detschmann.

The sky was still clear when the team set off again at 4am, so they chose to keep going. “After a while, we finally reached the final slope, just 300m below the summit,” Siegrist wrote. By now, they knew they were going to make it. They reached the top at 7:44am, six days after arriving in Base Camp, and just in time to hurry down as the storm approached.

The climbers descended via the 1985 Japanese route (see topo below), and reached their base camp tents as it started to snow.

Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (478 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.
  • Recent findings suggest that initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending.
  • Their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.

Recent findings suggest that initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending. The younger climber disputes this, saying they turned back near an alpine hut at 3,454m because his companion felt ill.

Their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14. The pair had no previous experience with such a serious mountain but had prepared by reading websites, watching videos, training physically, and asking others for tips. They did carry crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a rope, a belay device, and extra clothing.

In a recent development, it took them a long time before they decided to turn around. The descent went well at first, but one spot seemed too dangerous to them. To get around it, they followed someone else’s tracks in the snow, but these suddenly disappeared. While looking for a way, they got stuck in deep snow. The older boy called for help at around 6:30pm on November 15, according to Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.at.

Industry observers note that at first, rescuers tried to guide the pair down by phone. More than two hours later, the boys were still stuck, so a helicopter was dispatched. The rescuers found the pair, exhausted, disoriented, and hypothermic, at around 2,800m.

It has been revealed that A rescue helicopter brings the teens to safety. Photo: Mountain Rescue KALS.

Yesterday, rescue leader Peter Tembler criticized their lack of alpine experience and preparation. He told the German Press Agency that the pair lacked sufficient experience for the terrain and winter conditions. He also criticized their late-night departure.

Industry observers note that according to Tembler, a section that normally takes four to five hours took them almost 12. Other climbers reportedly advised them against continuing.

Tembler believes an increasing number of inexperienced people are attempting serious alpine routes, sometimes encouraged by social media accounts that downplay the difficulty. The disagreement has become a public debate about risk-taking, responsibility, and rescue operations.

According to recent reports, as Austria’s highest peak, Grossglockner is a magnet for climbers of all stripes and has more than its share of controversy. In January 2025, a man abandoned his less experienced girlfriend high on the mountain. She froze to death, and an Austrian court later convicted him of manslaughter for leaving her behind. This summer, an altercation occurred on Grossglockner in which a guide insulted a passing climber and nearly pushed him off a cliff. At the same time, veteran alpinists are still setting bold upcoming routes here.

Industry observers note that according to Der Standard, Grossglockner gets 8,000 to 9,000 ascents each year, with an average of two dozen rescues annually. Between 2005 and 2025, 29 climbers have died on the mountain.

Weekend Warm-Up: Hurricane Chase

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (464 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.
  • The storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective.
  • “That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.

The storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective. As the climate changes and disrupts weather patterns, tornadoes are no longer limited to traditional seasons and ranges.

“That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”.

Driving into a potential tornado in Montana. Photo: Screenshot.

It has been revealed that with hurricane and tornado seasons now overlapping, the duo is forced to split up to cover the widest possible area and collect the most data. For the tornadoes, this means deploying a probe into the funnel.

Up north in the High Plains of the U.S. West and Midwest, Timmer and his dog Gizmo narrowly miss storm after storm. Gizmo is better company but is a very poor navigator, while Timmer isn’t much better. He constantly makes wrong turns as he tries to navigate, drive, and prepare equipment. He does take the time to explain the basic weather science behind what he is failing to catch, such as the conditions that created the baseball-sized hail pummeling his windshield.

Timmer and Gizmo drive through the aftermath of a powerful tornado in the Black Hills of North Dakota. Photo: Screenshot.

Sources indicate that in Florida, Theiss sleeps in his car to maintain a constant vigil along the coast. Our current scientific abilities, he explains, allow us to track the movement of hurricane systems with decent accuracy. But predicting their strength is much more difficult. Systems can suddenly turn deadly or fizzle out with equally short notice. In this case, the terrible-looking storm comes to nothing. He heads back up north to rejoin Timmer and Gizmo.

Gizmo buffeted by fierce winds. Photo: Screenshot.

Recent findings suggest that the reunited trio prepares for a final effort, complete with a windshield-replacement sequence. They immediately drive into the gathering storm, passing through a hail core which, of course, destroys the new windshield. The Lord giveth and taketh away, et cetera. Soon they’re racing on a near-empty tank, as the powerful storm threatens to touch down at any moment.

Recent findings suggest that it’s their last chance this season to deploy the probe. When, after a long, tense chase, they actually manage to do it, both erupt into cheers. Gizmo appears unmoved, despite the fact that this ground probe, deployed in a storm of this type, in this area, has never been deployed before and is sure to yield valuable scientific data.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Richard Carlos Skidmore, 66, of the United States, was found dead in his tent on Mera Peak on Sunday, November 22, after summiting the 6,476m mountain the previous morning.

According to Solukhumbu district police, he reached the summit at approximately 10am on Saturday, November 21, and descended to the high camp at around 5,800m, where he spent the night.

It has been revealed that he was found dead the next morning. Past Mera Peak climbers have suggested on social media that it was unusual to overnight in the high camp after summiting so early in the day.

It has been revealed that his body was evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu for an autopsy. The cause of death remains undetermined. An initial report raised the possibility of altitude-related illness or a cardiac event, but neither has been established medically.

Recent findings suggest that skidmore previously summited Lobuche Peak in 2024, according to the Everest Chronicle and the Italian Alpine Club’s publication Lo Scarpone. So he had previous Himalayan climbing experience above 6,000m.

The Himalayan Database does include Mera Peak, but its coverage of popular trekking peaks is selective. However, it notes that since 2018, four people have died on Mera Peak, not counting Skidmore.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Three Polish climbers have established a new line on the north face of one of the Tien Shan’s best-known climbing peaks.
  • Michal Makowski, Robert Paluch, and Rafal Zając took 11 hours to climb their new 850m line on 4,777m Free Korea Peak, in Kyrgyzstan’s northern Tien Shan Mountains.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Three Polish climbers have established a new line on the north face of one of the Tien Shan’s best-known climbing peaks.

Michal Makowski, Robert Paluch, and Rafal Zając took 11 hours to climb their new 850m line on 4,777m Free Korea Peak, in Kyrgyzstan’s northern Tien Shan Mountains. They then spent a further 11 hours returning to base camp.

They named the route The Polish Barber, after pioneer American climber Henry Barber, who soloed the wall in 1976. Their line shares the first 250–300m with Barber’s, Makowski told ExplorersWeb.

In a recent development, “According to the information I have, [the remaining 600-650m] was previously unclimbed and had never been attempted by another team,” noted Makowski. “We reached the summit ridge and then began rappelling down from there.

According to recent reports, corona Hut, the team’s base camp. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu.

Industry observers note that free Korea Peak — Pik Svobodnaya Koreya in Russian — was already famous among mountaineers in the former Soviet Union because of its 900m north wall. in 2018, Russian climber Valery Balesin suggested that it was no longer possible to find newly introduced lines on this well-known face, although advances in steep ice-climbing techniques have clearly opened new possibilities.

“My friends and I researched Free Korea Peak and realized that part of the north face still has unclimbed terrain,” said Makowski.

In a recent development, on the Polish Barber route. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu.

Their route was almost completely ice climbing. The crux came midway up the wall, when they faced a particularly steep section of ice that they graded at Alpine Ice 4+. The rest of the route was 3/3+. Fortunately, “protection on the Polish Barber was really good, except for the last 150m, where ice was pretty thin and crusty,” stated Makowski.

Sources indicate that climbing by moonlight. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu.

Despite its former popularity, they had the valley almost to themselves during their week in camp. There was just one Russian group doing a tourist trek up nearby Corona Peak.

Recent findings suggest that A scrambly section on Free Korea Peak. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu.

#159481. Ukrainian Solos Upcoming Route in Gokyo Valley, Near Everest

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (302 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Ukrainian Solos Upcoming Route in Gokyo Valley, Near Everest

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (302 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that mykyta Balabanov of Ukraine has soloed a new route on the northeast face of Nepal’s Phari Lapcha (6,017m).
  • Balabanov is still trekking back to Lukla, but has given ExplorersWeb some details and photos about this impressive new route.
  • The Ukrainian set off on his own up an unclimbed line on the northeast face on November 19.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that mykyta Balabanov of Ukraine has soloed a new route on the northeast face of Nepal’s Phari Lapcha (6,017m). Also known as Machhermo Peak, it sits 24km west of Everest in the Gokyo Valley.

Balabanov is still trekking back to Lukla, but has given ExplorersWeb some details and photos about this impressive new route.

The Ukrainian set off on his own up an unclimbed line on the northeast face on November 19. He made two bivouacs on the way up and one more on the descent.

“The level of difficulty is hard to tell, as always when solo, but I’d say it was around 80° on ice, M5+, 5c on rock, and lots of poor snow!” Balavanov mentioned.

He estimates the new route is 1,200m long, and spans some 850 vertical meters from base to summit.

Recent findings suggest that rough topo of Balabanov’s solo route on the northeast face of Phari Lapcha. Photo: Mykyta Balabanov.

Another side of Phari Lapcha saw action just one day before Balabanov, when U.S. guide Bennie Lieber led Canadian Emma Deguara up the Stone(d) Yeti route on the south face.

Sources indicate that “I was not related to that climb, as I climbed alone after approaching from a different valley,” Balabanov explained. “However, I saw their tracks on the summit and spotted their bivy place at the bottom of the south face.”.

Lieber and Deguara made the second ascent of their chosen route. “While the technical grade (M3, AI2+) is easily digestible, the room for mistakes, due to exposure, is zero,” Lieber said.

Mykyta Balabanov and fellow Ukrainian Mikhail Fomino opened a newly introduced route on Ama Dablam in 2024, but they first became widely known for their new route on the Southeast Ridge of Annapurna III in 2021.

Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1239 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the U.S.
  • Sources indicate that the complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections.
  • It has been revealed that BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the U.S. Senate plans to vote this week on a bill aimed at easing America’s affordability crisis and fighting climate change that hunting and fishing groups worry will also erode many of the nation’s bedrock conservation laws.

Sources indicate that the complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections. BAAJA also, however, ties jobs and household bills with curtailing public-lands protections. And in a twist that’s perplexing many conservation groups, the bill is co-sponsored by Sens. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Mike Lee (R-Utah), two lawmakers known for being on nearly opposite ends of the public-lands spectrum.

It has been revealed that BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. In practice, the legislation would raise the standard for whether projects approved by one administration can be revoked by a future administration.

Sources indicate that that means an industrial solar project permitted by one president, for example, could not be stymied by a future president intent on preventing renewables. It also speeds up permitting processes and cuts red tape for everything from energy projects to landscape-scale changes like prescribed fire.

But sportsmen and conservationists say the bill would not just expedite climate or environmentally friendly projects. BAAJA would also make it much harder — or potentially impossible — for an administration to overturn leases or approvals for projects as controversial as hyperscale data centers on public lands or mines in the same watersheds as sensitive wilderness areas. It’s a bill that prioritizes development, many observers say, at the cost of the very “red tape” that has been responsible for conserving many of the country’s most priceless fish, wildlife, and wild places.

It has been revealed that “I understand this is a big, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have. But I negotiated the deal based on what was actually possible to get signed into law,” Heinrich wrote in an email to Outdoor Life. “Because when I say climate change is an existential threat, I mean it. And I will not let an opportunity to do something about it pass by.”.

It has been revealed that conservationists like Ingrid Lyons, executive director of Save the Boundary Waters, understand the need for stability around permitting development. The whiplash between issuing and revoking permits for public land development projects every time an administration changes has likely hurt the U.S.’s ability to move forward with vital energy projects, including in renewables like wind and solar.

Industry observers note that but she fears this bill could instead cement the creation of controversial projects like a copper-sulfide mine at the headwaters of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or a copper-molybdenum-gold mine in the salmon-rich waters of Alaska’s Bristol Bay. Permits for projects like these have been denied, among other complications, because of environmental risk. If permits are reissued in similar scenarios, legislation like BAAJA could prevent future administrations from stopping development in places that truly need protection.

“What about landscape certainty?” Lyons claims. “We’re overlooking in some ways the impact to communities that are relying on protection and not just projects.”.

The conservation community has become increasingly vocal in its opposition to the bill since Heinrich and Lee partnered with Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), and Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), to introduce the legislation in late September. Lee has a clear track record of supporting public land sales and undermining existing public-lands conservation, including 2025’s attempt to include federal land sales in the One Significant Beautiful Bill.

Industry observers note that A lengthy version of BAAJA is before the Senate as of Tuesday. The current bill includes a variety of red flags for hunters, anglers, tribes, endangered-species advocates, and other conservationists.

Some of the main points include:.

The Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership acknowledged the need for permit reform but mentioned in a statement that “progress should not come at the expense of the conservation safeguards and public review that give hunters and anglers a voice in how our lands and waters are managed.”.

For Lyons, it comes down to the potential unintended consequences of sweeping legislation like BAAJA.

“We need to be exceptionally aware of the implications of this bill, which could be that a lot of these really beloved places could have projects many communities have worked really hard to oppose cemented into place.”.

Many in the conservation community were surprised by the bill’s sponsors, given Heinrich’s history as a sportsman and conservationist who regularly defends public lands and sensitive places, and Lee’s general position as a proponent of development and public-lands sell-off.

It has been revealed that but in Heinrich’s statement to Outdoor Life, he emphasizes the impact of climate change on our planet, including the places where people hunt, hike, bike and camp. Independent modeling, he mentioned, predicts the bill will lead to a 20 percent reduction in power sector emissions, or the “equivalent to taking 39 coal plants offline for 10 years.”.

“You cannot protect a trout stream without paying attention to the warming temperatures and declining flows that threaten it,” he wrote. “You cannot protect wildlife habitat while ignoring the impacts of increasingly severe drought and wildfire. We need to reduce emissions, and that means getting more clean energy onto the grid.”.

Recent findings suggest that in an Oct. 30 op-ed in the Albuquerque Journal, Heinrich explained how New Mexico’s SunZia Wind and Transmission project took 17 years to permit and build.

He also pushed back on what he called misinformation about the bill, stating he doesn’t believe data centers should be on public land. The bill also requires large scale data center operators to pay the full cost of electricity consumed by the facility.

The Izaak Walton League’s conservation director, Kate Miller, thinks each of the bill’s sponsors are acting in good faith and trying to do what is right for their constituents. Many projects, including those aimed at restoring forests and wildlife habitat, have been held up by permitting delays. Something like BAAJA could move those forward.

It has been revealed that but Miller would have liked to see these issues tackled individually instead of in a massive bill. And while she hopes that, if the bill passes, the administration will respect existing laws, the past two years has brought an onslaught of changes to most of the nation’s bedrock environmental laws including the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act.

According to recent reports, “We want to make sure what comes out is not something that sacrifices those core protections that allow us to have healthy waters and habitats,” Miller indicates. “That we don’t sacrifice one for the other.”.

Industry observers note that while the Senate is fast tracking the bill before the next Congress begins in January, it must move through the Senate and the House, and any changes be agreed upon by both chambers before the bill would land on President Trump’s desk. Meanwhile, both industry and conservation groups say they’re working to lobby lawmakers for changes and amendments. As a result, several conservation organizations declined to comment for this story.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An Idaho Fish and Game commissioner just made a deal to avoid poaching and trespassing charges related to an illegal elk hunt last season.
  • 9 eastern Idaho’s representative, Brody Harshbarger, agreed to plead guilty to two of seven charges of wildlife violations in exchange for having the remaining charges dropped.
  • Sources indicate that his guilty pleas are for hunting without a tag and shooting across the road, according to local news outlets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Idaho Fish and Game commissioner just made a deal to avoid poaching and trespassing charges related to an illegal elk hunt last season.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 9 eastern Idaho’s representative, Brody Harshbarger, agreed to plead guilty to two of seven charges of wildlife violations in exchange for having the remaining charges dropped.

Sources indicate that his guilty pleas are for hunting without a tag and shooting across the road, according to local news outlets. The dismissed charges include two for poaching, trespass, motorized aid and failure to retrieve game. Both of the killed animals were bull elk, one antlerless and the other a 6×6 which was on private property. Harshbarger was accompanied by another man, Eric Murphy, at the time.

Related: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Charged with Poaching Elk, Trespassing, Says He’ll ‘Voluntarily Postpone’ Duties.

“Neither Brody Harshbarger nor Eric Murphy called the landowners to request permission to retrieve the six-point bull and did not make a reasonable effort to retrieve the six-point bull,” according to investigation documents obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun. “Neither individual had permission to be shooting onto the private property in violation of Idaho Code.”.

In a recent development, harshbarger had already filled his elk tag the weekend before the two bulls were shot. His hometown, Ashton, is in the same county where the violations took place. That same county, Fremont, borders Yellowstone National Park and is in the region Harshbarger represents on the state’s seven-person commission. That commission sets statewide hunting, fishing, and trapping seasons plus bag limits and other regulations based on recommendations and research supplied by Idaho Department of Fish and Game scientists.

Each member of the commission, most often a resident hunter and/or fisherman, is appointed by the governor for a term of four years with a two-term maximum. The commission meets at least four times a year. Harshbarger hasn’t attended those meetings since his case opened after a tip received through the department’s Citizens Against Poaching in December. He hasn’t resigned and the Governor hasn’t dismissed him, but his profile has been removed from the commission’s website.

It has been revealed that “The Governor’s office is aware of Commissioner Harshbarger’s plea agreement,” Gov. Brad Little’s spokeswoman Emily Callihan told the Sun. “Gov. Little will be working with the Idaho Department of Fish and Game and stakeholders in the coming days to ensure the responsibilities of the position are fulfilled.”.

Industry observers note that harshbarger was appointed to the commission in 2024. His sentencing for illegal activities in 2025 is scheduled for Dec. 9. With the upcoming plea deal and the number of charges reduced, the fine is expected to be $500 plus a one-year loss of hunting privileges.

#159449. Jeff Sturgis’ Secrets for Hunting Big Whitetail Bucks

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1078 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Jeff Sturgis’ Secrets for Hunting Big Whitetail Bucks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies.
  • Recent findings suggest that this summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks.
  • Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies. He’s honed these strategies through decades of hard hunting and consulting on his clients’ properties. He’s also tested them on his own 170-acre property in the bluff country of southern Minnesota (you can follow him on his YouTube channel, Whitetail Habitat Solutions).

Recent findings suggest that this summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks. In the video above, Sturgis runs through his five favorite setups and explains how he hunts them. Some of these setups take an immense amount of work and expense to develop. Others require minimal habitat work but a deep understanding of deer behavior.

Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.

Everyone talks about “buck bedding areas” but many hunters have only a vague understanding of them. The important point, Sturgis notes, is that bucks do not like to bed near a lot of commotion, and that includes commotion from other deer. For example, does will often bed near major food sources. It’s convenient for them to get up from their bed and stroll right into a large food plot or ag field.

Mature bucks don’t like to bed around a mass of other deer. So buck beds will be found farther away from main food sources — even if there is prime bedding habitat right by those food sources. So just because you’re seeing a lot of does and young bucks in an area doesn’t mean it’s a good spot for mature bucks. In fact, it could mean the opposite.

By crossing off areas where mature bucks won’t bed — again, areas with high pressure and activity — you can narrow down where they will bed. Sturgis isn’t afraid to hunt near buck bedding areas, but he does so sparingly. And when he does, he often takes his target buck.

Recent findings suggest that when you see deer consistently coming to a significant food plot or agricultural field during daylight hours, it’s tempting to just hunt that major food source. Sturgis will hunt the big “holding plot” on his property, but only when he’s able to do so without spooking deer. He’s got a Redneck blind at the edge of the plot, which has an access route that is completely blocked by screening cover. He can get into and out of the blind with deer in the field — and never spook them. But that setup means he’s only able to hunt the big holding plot during gun season, even if there are target bucks hitting it during bow season.

It has been revealed that sturgis considers the holding plot the cornerstone of his entire property. So long as deer feel safe feeding there, he’s in the game. Even if he happens to bump a buck out of its bedding area, that deer is likely to switch bedding areas but still come to the holding plot to feed. This means that Sturgis can keep hunting that buck.

On the flipside, if he blows out the holding plot, it throws off deer behavior for the entire property, and that could be detrimental to his entire season. In some ways, he treats the holding plot like a sanctuary.

Sturgis has a ton of videos about how to set up and hunt waterholes. He creates his waterhole setups in the woods in traditional rut funnels. These waterholes give deer a reason to come within bow range and to stop there. Sturgis and his wife, Jen, have some of their best big-buck hunts over waterholes.

Sources indicate that these setups are relatively easy to implement, assuming you can get some kind of water tank into the woods where you hunt. They’re great places for all-day sits during the heart of the rut.

We all love to be in the woods before sunrise and to hear the telltale sound of a buck marching into range just after shooting light. But in some cases it’s impossible to hunt a spot first thing in the morning without spooking deer. These are often areas near field edges — deer are still in the fields feeding in the dark.

In these scenarios Sturgis will simply enter the stand an hour or so after daylight when deer have left the field. This allows him to slip in undetected and have several hours of quality hunting before leaving again in the evening. These are usually high-probability sits during the rut.

The main principle that Sturgis’ hunting strategy revolves around is to not overpressure mature deer. He wants major bucks to do their thing: rut, establish their dominance, and move around the habitat, during daylight hours. He lets his Tactacam trail cameras do the monitoring, and he picks his sits carefully. Of course we all love being in the woods and Sturgis does too. So he has stands that are very low impact for those times when he or someone in his family just wants to hunt — and you never know, a mature buck could stroll by any time.

But his approach is much more surgical when really targeting a specific deer.

Recent findings suggest that one of the many things I learned from Sturgis is that all of the knowledge (and much more) outlined above has been built into the Habitat IQ app. This app allows the user to draw in habitat features (like food sources, water, timber, and roads) into their own property. The program then uses a powerful algorithm, built off of Sturgis’ knowledge, to make habitat improvement suggestions and predict deer movement.

For example, if you don’t have any useful water sources on your property, the app will suggest adding some waterholes, and give you an idea about the best areas to place them.

Related: Here’s What Most Hunters Get Wrong About Whitetails, According to Jeff Sturgis.

It has been revealed that the app is basically a digital version of Sturgis’ habitat/hunting consulting business. The more data you add into it, the better information you get back. I think this will be an incredibly powerful tool for anyone who is looking to implement the concepts that Sturgis has proven out over the course of 20-plus years of consulting on deer properties.
